opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so that was one of the findings that really surprised us. When we compared models across tasks, the gap between a model fine-tuned for extractive question answering and a general-purpose generative model doing the "same" task was huge, often an order of magnitude or more in energy per query.

The way I make sense of it is to look at what each model is actually doing. An extractive QA model, say a fine-tuned BERT-style encoder, takes the question and a passage and predicts a start and end position. That's essentially one forward pass, and the model is relatively small. A generative model has to produce the answer token by token. Every new token is another pass through the network, and that network is often billions of parameters. So you're paying for the larger model and for the autoregressive decoding.

There's also a "doing everything" tax. A big generative model is trained to write poems, code, summaries, and to answer trivia. When you use it for extractive QA, you're running all that general capacity for a task that needs a fraction of it. It's like taking a semi truck to pick up a carton of milk.

What worries me is that the field and industry have shifted toward a default of "just use the big generative model for everything," because it's convenient. You don't have to fine-tune anything, you just prompt it. But every query has an energy and carbon cost, and at the scale of millions or billions of queries, those differences really add up.

So my takeaway isn't that generative models are bad. It's that we should be intentional. If your task is well defined, like extracting an answer from a document, classifying sentiment, or tagging entities, a smaller task-specific model is often just as good, sometimes better, and far more efficient. We need to make those trade-offs visible so people can choose the right tool, not just the biggest one.

r001.rationale: The response says the energy gap is often an order of magnitude or more, but it does not state the specific figure of up to 30 times as much energy.

r002.rationale: It contrasts extractive QA’s single pass predicting text positions with generative QA’s token-by-token output, requiring repeated passes through a larger model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was actually one of the things that surprised us the most when we did the study, because we compared models doing the same task — question answering — but doing it in two fundamentally different ways. The extractive models, like a BERT-style model fine-tuned on SQuAD, are basically doing a pointing operation. You give them a context and a question, and they find the span in the text that answers it. They're not generating anything new. And then you have the generative models, the Flan-T5s and the LLaMAs and so on, that are producing the answer token by token.

And the difference in energy was not small. We're talking orders of magnitude in some cases. The extractive models were in the range of, you know, a few hundredths of a kilowatt-hour per thousand queries, and the generative ones were ten, twenty, thirty times more for the exact same question. And the thing is, from the user's perspective, the output looks pretty much the same. You ask "who wrote this book" and you get "Jane Austen" either way.

So how I make sense of it is really about what the model is doing under the hood. With extraction, the computation is bounded — the model does one forward pass and produces a classification over positions in the input. With generation, every token you produce requires another forward pass through the whole network, and the model has to be big enough to actually carry all that world knowledge and language ability around with it, even if you're only asking it something trivial. You're essentially paying for a general-purpose capability that you're not using. It's like driving a semi-truck to pick up a loaf of bread.

And I think the broader point we were trying to make is that there's been this collapse of everything into generation. Five years ago, if you had a question answering problem, you'd train a task-specific model. Now the default is to just prompt a large language model, and nobody really stops to ask whether that's the right tool. Sometimes it is — if your task is genuinely open-ended, generation makes sense. But a huge fraction of what people are deploying generative models for is stuff that classification or extraction would handle perfectly well, at a fraction of the cost. So the energy difference, to me, is really a symptom of a design choice that's become invisible because it's the default.

r001.rationale: It says generative models use “ten, twenty, thirty times more” energy for the same question, communicating that the difference can reach 30 times.

r002.rationale: It contrasts extraction as a single pass that selects a span from existing text with generation, which requires another full-network pass for each output token.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is what you’re asking the model to do. With extractive question answering, you give it a passage and a question, and its job is to identify where the answer is in that passage. It’s a very constrained task.

With a generative model, you’re asking it to produce an answer token by token. Even if the answer is already in the passage, it’s using this much more general capability to generate language, and each additional token requires more computation.

So the comparison is really about whether you need that generality for the task you’re doing. A generative model can do lots of things, which is useful, but that flexibility can come with an energy cost. If all you need is to pull an answer out of a document, a model trained specifically for that task can be much more efficient. The size of the models and the length of the generated response matter, too, so it’s not one fixed difference across every setup.

r001.rationale: It says generative models can carry an energy cost, but gives no claim that they use up to 30 times as much energy for the same question.

r002.rationale: It contrasts identifying the answer in an existing passage with generating an answer token by token, noting that each additional token requires more computation.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is: what are you asking the model to do? With extractive question answering, you give it a passage and it identifies where the answer is in that passage. It’s a very constrained task. A generative model is producing an answer token by token, and each of those tokens requires another pass through the model.

So even if the answer looks similar to the person asking the question, the computation behind it can be very different. You’re using this general-purpose system, which can do all kinds of things, for a task that a much more specialized model can handle. That flexibility has an energy cost.

That doesn’t mean generation is never useful. But if what you need is to find an answer in a document, it’s worth asking whether you need a model to generate anything at all.

r001.rationale: The response says generation has an energy cost but does not state the comparison of up to 30 times as much energy.

r002.rationale: It explains that extractive QA locates an answer in a passage, while generative QA produces the answer token by token, requiring another model pass for each token.
